column15: And “miggen” means Hashem encircled them, enclosing them as in a dungeon, placing a bridle and bit in their mouth that they could not proceed on their way, rather delivering them into Avraham's hand to vanquish them. Akin to what is taught in the Talmud (Berakhot 57a) regarding dreams of wine: there is one who drinks it and it is good for him, and one who drinks it and it is bad for him; for a Torah scholar it is always good, even if placed in an iron collar—they added protection unto his protection.

column11: Megillah 11a: ‘The opening verse continues, stating that Ahasuerus reigned “over seven and twenty and a hundred provinces” (Esther 1:1). Rav Ḥisda said: This verse should be understood as follows: At first he reigned over seven provinces; and then he reigned over twenty more; and finally he reigned over another hundred. The Gemara asks: However, if that is so, with regard to the similarly worded verse: “And the years of the life of Amram were seven and thirty and a hundred years” (Exodus 6:20), what would you expound from it? The Gemara answers: It is different here, in the book of Esther, as this part of the verse is entirely superfluous. Since it is already written: “From Hodu to Cush,” why then do I…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Megillah 11a) to illuminate his exposition here (“And Ahasuerus was named because the faces of Israel were blackened in his days (Megillah 11a), meaning merely a temporary, external blackness upon the face; and afterward: "The Jews had light" [Esther 8:16]—this is...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: This is termed the perception of the “ends of the earth”— meaning they recognized that even within earthly, mundane actions—which operate naturally—there exists a miraculous course and the direct salvation of Hashem. This represents the outer perimeter of the structure of the blessed Hashem’s salvation and His revealed miracles in this world, for the attribute of Malkhut is the final attribute in every complete spiritual configuration, as is known, and its purpose is to demonstrate His sovereignty among the lower realms and within the terrestrial governance of this physical world.
column15: “And the Lord said: My spirit shall not abide in man forever, for that he also is flesh; therefore shall his days be a hundred and twenty years.” It is stated in Tractate Chullin (139b): Where is Moses alluded to in the Torah? In the verse: “For that he also (be-shagam = 345 = Moshe) is flesh”; and it is necessary to understand: What was the Gemara's question? Is it a small matter that Moses is mentioned countless times throughout the Torah?

column11: Esther 8:16: ‘The Jews enjoyed light and gladness, happiness and honor.’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Esther 8:16) to illuminate his exposition here (“and afterward: "The Jews had light" [Esther 8:16]—this is Torah (Megillah 16b), meriting to re-accept it out of love (Shabbat 88a). And suspending the mountain like a vat was over the Oral Torah (Tanchuma Noach 3),...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: And the Men of the Great Assembly who instituted: "that these days should be remembered and kept throughout every generation" (Esther 9:28); meant that holiness be permanently engraved within Jewish hearts every year through remembering and fulfilling the mitzvos of the day; the Blessed Name having consented unto their ordinance (Megillah 7a), wherefore we bless over the Megillah: "Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us"; infusing holiness into the heart to merit even now light and gladness.
column15: Therefore it is written subsequently: “And the Lord God caused a deep sleep to fall upon the man” — meaning that during sleep his supernal vitality ascended, leaving merely the outer garment of life, which is awe. As occurred at Mount Sinai when Hashem revealed Himself with the shofar and torches—the aspect of Love—showing that their souls were bound to the highest heavens; and afterward when the shofar ceased, only awe remained within them having beheld His great majesty.

column11: Megillah 16b: ‘§ The Gemara returns to its explanation of the Megilla. The verse states: “The Jews had light and gladness, and joy and honor” (Esther 8:16). Rav Yehuda said: “Light”; this is referring to the Torah that they once again studied. And similarly it says: “For the mitzva is a lamp and the Torah is light” (Proverbs 6:23). “Gladness” [simḥa]; this is referring to the Festivals that they once again observed. And similarly it says: “And you shall be glad [vesamakhta] on your Festival” (Deuteronomy 16:14). “Joy” [sasson]; this is referring to circumcision, as they once again circumcised their sons. And similarly it says: “I rejoice [sas] at Your word” (Psalms 119:162), which the Sages understood…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Megillah 16b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and afterward: "The Jews had light" [Esther 8:16]—this is Torah (Megillah 16b), meriting to re-accept it out of love (Shabbat 88a). And suspending the mountain like a vat was over the Oral Torah (Tanchuma Noach 3),...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: And "joy" (Sason, Esther 8:16)—this is circumcision (Megillah 16b); this embodying the supreme inborn sanctity of Israel which distinguishes them from the nations; as the Sages stated in Nedarim (31b): even uncircumcised Israelites are legally termed circumcised, meaning even if in physical fact they are uncircumcised; and "even though he has sinned, he is an Israelite" (Sanhedrin 44a), his essential root never altering; whereas circumcised gentiles are legally termed uncircumcised (ibid.).
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:7
column15: As it is written (Psalms 46:5): "There is a river, the streams whereof make glad the city of God", and a 'tower' is an elevated monument visible from afar, meaning that the central unifying nucleus would be embodied among them and protect them. And this they enacted after having observed the fate of the Generation of the Flood, where Hashem wiped out all existence from upon the face of the ground, from man to beast, and nothing remained of them except Noach and his sons, through whom the world was rebuilt anew.

column11: Shabbat 88a: ‘The Gemara cites additional homiletic interpretations on the topic of the revelation at Sinai. The Torah says, “And Moses brought forth the people out of the camp to meet God; and they stood at the lowermost part of the mount” (Exodus 19:17). Rabbi Avdimi bar Ḥama bar Ḥasa said: the Jewish people actually stood beneath the mountain, and the verse teaches that the Holy One, Blessed be He, overturned the mountain above the Jews like a tub, and said to them: If you accept the Torah, excellent, and if not, there will be your burial. Rav Aḥa bar Ya’akov said: From here there is a substantial caveat to the obligation to fulfill the Torah. The Jewish people can claim that they were coerced into…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 88a) to illuminate his exposition here (“and afterward: "The Jews had light" [Esther 8:16]—this is Torah (Megillah 16b), meriting to re-accept it out of love (Shabbat 88a). And suspending the mountain like a vat was over the Oral Torah (Tanchuma Noach 3),...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: And so the primary salvation emerged through the cure seeded at Ahasuerus's banquet "when the heart of the king was merry with wine" (Esther 1:10); for wine accomplishes much (Sotah 7a): on the side of evil breeding licentiousness, for one drinks and it is disastrous for him, while another drinks and it is beneficial; for "wine and fragrance make one wise" (ibid.), this being the sublime wine of Torah; this being the gladdening wine drunk on Purim when Israel re-accepted the Torah out of love.
column15: For whenever this primordial light reveals itself directly, it becomes instantly apparent that there is no true existence in the universe other than the Blessed Name alone. And as taught in the Gemara (Megillah 19b): Had there remained in the cave where Moses and Elijah stood even an opening the size of the eye of a fine needle, they would have been unable to survive before the brilliance of that illumination.

column11: Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 3: ‘The Israelites did not accept the Torah until the Holy One, blessed be He, arched the mountain over them like a vessel, as it is said: And they stood beneath the mountain (Exod. 19:17). R. Dimi the son of Hama stated that the Holy One, blessed be He, told Israel: If you accept the Torah, well and good; but if not, your grave will be there. If you should say that He arched the mountain over them because of the Written Law, isn’t it true that as soon as He said to them, “Will you accept the Torah?” they all responded, “We will do and hear,” because the Written Law was brief and required no striving and suffering, but rather He threatened them because of the Oral Law. After all, it contains…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 3) to illuminate his exposition here (“And suspending the mountain like a vat was over the Oral Torah (Tanchuma Noach 3), which requires exhausting toil; and at Sinai all merited "face to face Hashem spoke with you" [Deuteronomy 5:4], like the prophecy of...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: And the task in the month of Marcheshvan is to assume the yoke of Torah in truth; and the essence of the yoke of Torah is in the study of the Oral Torah, which entails great exertion and sleepless nights, and one who covets wealth and pleasure cannot master the Oral Torah, as is stated (Tanchuma, Noach 3). And we learned: ‘Whoever accepts upon himself the yoke of Torah—they remove from him, etc.’; and therefore most harsh decrees threaten in this month, so that people will embrace the Torah in truth.
column15: “And Noah only remained alive.” In Tanchuma (Noach 9): Rav Huna said: He emerged groaning and spitting blood on account of the cold; not following Rabbi Yochanan from Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yose HaGelili who said that a lion struck him — because all who entered the Ark returned to concealment at their root like a fetus in its mother's womb, natural biological forces ceasing throughout that year, as in Midrash Rabbah that the constellations ceased their influence for twelve months.

column11: Deuteronomy 5:4: ‘Face to face GOD spoke to you on the mountain out of the fire—’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Deuteronomy 5:4) to illuminate his exposition here (“and at Sinai all merited "face to face Hashem spoke with you" [Deuteronomy 5:4], like the prophecy of Moses, and had they remained on that level, they would not have needed any toil in the Oral Torah at all; but sin...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: And this is the internal core, just as the heart is the interior to the limbs which are external to it, clear perception dwelling in the heart where awe resides (Yoma 72b). Wherefore Scripture states: "for Hashem searches all hearts," and our Sages stated (Sanhedrin 106b): the Merciful One desires the heart, corresponding to: "what does Hashem your God require of you, but to fear [Hashem your God]" [Deuteronomy 10:12], regarding which the Sages remarked (Berakhot 33b): for Moses, who embodies lucid perception, this is a minor matter.
column15: And regarding this the Zohar stated: “Noah and those with him were hidden from sight”; as taught in Tanchuma (Noach 9): throughout that entire year Noah saw no sleep with his eyes — for sleep represents forgetfulness, and Noah saw no sleep, meaning he did not forget himself for a single moment to imagine that he was an independent creature severed from the Blessed Name, but throughout that entire era of the Flood he continually enfolded himself into his Root, standing face-to-face before the Blessed Name in lucid and transparent clarity.

column11: Exodus 20:16: ‘“You speak to us,” they said to Moses, “and we will obey; but let not God speak to us, lest we die.”’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Exodus 20:16) to illuminate his exposition here (“but sin caused them to plead afterward: "let not God speak with us, lest we die" [Exodus 20:16], their soul departing at His word (Shabbat 88b), because the body was not yet refined like that of Moses. Yet had they...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: Which was absorbed into its source like a small candle in a massive bonfire, until the people cried out, as in "let not God speak with us lest we die" (Exodus 20:16), and the fire abated. And then base lust was born within them, for the fiery blaze stems from the intense heat of love of Abraham our father for Hashem.
column15: For the underlying root of all temporal affairs in this world is words of Torah. And the Blessed Name instituted the six workdays in order that man might enclothe words of Torah within physical garments; and permission was granted to man to extend his boundary, introducing Torah into distant external garments and expanding according to his judgment, as written (Exodus 20:9): “Six days you shall labor, etc.”

column11: Shabbat 88b: ‘With regard to the revelation at Sinai, Rabbi Yoḥanan said: What is the meaning of that which is written: “The Lord gives the word; the women that proclaim the tidings are a great host” (Psalms 68:12)? It means that each and every utterance that emerged from the mouth of the Almighty divided into seventy languages, a great host. And, similarly, the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught with regard to the verse: “Behold, is My word not like fire, declares the Lord, and like a hammer that shatters a rock?” (Jeremiah 23:29). Just as this hammer breaks a stone into several fragments, so too, each and every utterance that emerged from the mouth of the Holy One, Blessed be He, divided into seventy…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 88b) to illuminate his exposition here (“their soul departing at His word (Shabbat 88b), because the body was not yet refined like that of Moses. Yet had they merited to hear all the Commandments from the Almighty, the entire body would have been refined,...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: The explanation: to self-aggrandize stems from desire/ambition, and this is tolerable within the camp of Israel; whereas to spite stems from malicious envy, which is utterly forbidden in Israel, and of which it is said 'better had his placenta inverted'. And the inversion of lust is achieved through envy, as explained; and therefore, one who separates from lust not for Heaven's sake, the hinge of Gehenna turns upon him, meaning, he stands at the very threshold of the punishment of the wicked.
column15: Here man must exercise restraint; this Black Fire consumes and restrains man from taking more than his allocated share, for excessive indulgence would overwhelm his mind and cause him to forget his divine Benefactor. And this is what is stated in the Zohar (Bereishit 15a): Botzina de-Kardinuta (the spark of darkness), meaning brilliant light cloaked in surrounding dark, and as in Zohar (22b): “In our likeness—that darkness which serves as a garment to the light, just as the body serves as a garment to the soul,” and further (23b): “Darkness is the black ink of Torah, light is the white parchment of Torah.”

column11: Sanhedrin 63b: ‘What is the meaning of the statement: “Those who sacrifice men kiss calves”? Rabbi Yitzḥak of the school of Rabbi Ami says: It means that priests of idol worship would set their eyes on the wealthy, and they would starve the calves that were objects of idol worship, and make statues in the image of those wealthy people, and place those statues next to the troughs of the calves, and they would take those calves outside. When the calves would see those wealthy people, whose image they were used to seeing near their troughs, they would run after them and paw them. At this point the priests would say to that wealthy person: The object of idol worship, the calf, desires you; let the Master…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 63b) to illuminate his exposition here (“wherefore faith is fixed in the hearts of Israel, who served idols only to permit licentiousness publicly (Sanhedrin 63b), driven by the lust of physical matter and not heresy against the faith, which is impossible...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: The yetzer desiring to inject this infinite passion into worldly lusts and extinguish the authentic holy yearning; craving worldly lusts boundlessly without satiation, where the number one thousand does not suffice. Wherefore the Philistines, seeking to inject into Delilah's heart the monetary greed of the yetzer, added beyond one thousand [offering 1,100]; and so with Micah's idol, the inception was his submersion in greed, through which he kicked against the root of Judaism.
column15: Just as we see that the Torah forbids gluttonous overeating (achilah gasah), as derived in Sanhedrin (63a) from “You shall not eat with the blood” regarding the rebellious son. Because even in permitted matters, excess indulgence is forbidden; except that with forbidden foods like swine, any minute portion consumed is inherently gluttonous; and so here, regarding this tree Hashem banned even the slightest particle, as explained regarding Pesach.

column11: Exodus 20:14: ‘You shall not covet your neighbor’s house: you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, or male or female slave, or ox or donkey, or anything that is your neighbor’s.’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Exodus 20:14) to illuminate his exposition here (“And with the final commandment "You shall not covet" [Exodus 20:14]—the end of action wedded to the initial thought, envying one's fellow's share— which is the root of the inclination obscuring "I am Hashem," the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: Rather, the meaning is: she offered an apology saying: I did not laugh in mockery or as one who disbelieves at all; but "because she feared," and out of holy fear lest she be unable to exert herself in divine service as is fitting for such a promise, she laughed; and such was indeed the truth according to her perspective; nevertheless this was accounted a denial before the Blessed Name Who knows the inward depths of her heart; knowing that she ought not to have feared this given the powerful intensity of her faith.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 14:13–14
column15: While in the depth of Lot's heart there was no divine service or fear, as there were born of him nations from whom Israel suffered, as brought in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 96b): “Ammon and Moab were the wicked neighbors of Jerusalem.” 3 And that he went to rescue Lot corresponds to “You shall not take the name of Hashem your God in vain” (Exodus 20:7).

column11: Shabbat 105b: ‘The Gemara asks: Say that you heard that Rabbi Yehuda rules that one is liable for performing a labor not needed for its own sake in the case of a constructive act; did you hear him deem one liable in the case of a destructive act? Rabbi Avin said: This case, where one rends his garment in anger, is also constructive, because in doing so he assuages his anger. Rending his garment calms him; therefore, it can be said that he derives benefit from the act of rending, and it is consequently a constructive act. The Gemara asks: And is it at all permitted to tear in that manner? Wasn’t it taught in a baraita that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says in the name of Ḥilfa bar Agra, who said in the name…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 105b) to illuminate his exposition here (“the way of the inclination being: today it says do this, until it says go serve idols (Shabbat 105b), all to fulfill physical lust; had they merited to receive it from the Almighty, covetousness would have been...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: Idolatry is the middle pillar, Tiferet of the husk flowing from Keter, the impulse to mimic divinity, which is idolatry. The right extreme is sexual immorality, depraved lust and love: "it is a perverted love (chesed)" [Leviticus 20:17]; and evil Gevurah is shedding innocent blood through violence. And twice the Sages taught: "Such is the way of the Evil Inclination: today it says do this, until it says worship idols": first in Shabbat (105b) regarding one who smashes vessels in anger, an accessory of bloodshed.
column15: On Shabbat, however, Malchut Shamayim is unveiled, pointing to the ultimate future when “Hashem alone shall be exalted on that day”; then any assertive human labor blemishes the revealed Oneness of the Creator; and man must strictly abide within the boundary ordained by Hashem, desisting from all autonomous physical creation; as in Zohar (Emor 94b): Rabbi Yitzchak asked: Why are they called the six days of chul (profane/secular)? Rabbi Yose replied: Because the world is then governed through divine emissaries.

column11: Ezekiel 36:26: ‘And I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit into you: I will remove the heart of stone from your body and give you a heart of flesh;’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Ezekiel 36:26) to illuminate his exposition here (“"I will give you a heart of flesh (basar)" [Ezekiel 36:26]—feeling bashful (boser), not coveting his fellow's share, and they would have needed no toil in the Oral Torah automatically; and they yearned to attain that...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: And likewise, a spirit summoned through necromancy does not ascend on Shabbat, even if the deceased was a gentile. For the Sabbath's rest and holiness originate from the very Creation of the universe, and the essential sanctity of the day itself applies equally to all inhabitants of the world, only that Hashem bestowed its active observance as a precious gift unto Israel.
column15: And there it appears that repentance is withheld from him, heaven forbid. The explanation of this—though our Sages taught that nothing stands before repentance—is: teshuvah rectifies when one recognizes his flaw and abandons the specific sin, repairing the exact place he blemished; and when the blemish has taken root in his mind, corrupting his consciousness, profound repentance is required to heal it at the root.

column11: Deuteronomy 5:25: ‘GOD heard the plea that you made to me, and GOD said to me, “I have heard the plea that this people made to you; they did well to speak thus.’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Deuteronomy 5:25) to illuminate his exposition here (“And the Blessed Name likewise willed it: "O that there were such a heart in them..." [Deuteronomy 5:25]; only that all operates in justice, man having been created to choose good freely, requiring at least an opening...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: For toward this service the nations were created, and when truth is unveiled in the Future they will consent to this status; but Amalek will never consent to this, being the absolute concentration of Esav's deceptive display of split hooves; his entire essence drawing power from this falsehood which holds sway in this world of deceit as long as the seed of Amalek endures.
column15: And this explains the Talmudic passage in Chullin (139b): “Where is Haman alluded to in the Torah? In the verse: ‘Hamin ha-etz (Is it from the tree) whereof I commanded you.’” The meaning is: the question was, how could such pitch darkness fall upon Israel as in the days of Haman, spawning such terror that they thought they would be utterly obliterated, heaven forbid, when they well knew Hashem bound His very Name to Israel, giving them the unbreakable plea: “What will You do for Your great Name!”?

column11: Avodah Zarah 4b: ‘And Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says: The Jewish people fashioned the Golden Calf (see Exodus, chapter 32) only to give a claim to penitents, as it is stated after the revelation at Sinai: “Who would give that they had such a heart as this always, to fear Me, and keep all My commandments, that it might be good for them, and with their children forever” (Deuteronomy 5:26). If the nation was truly at such a lofty spiritual state, how could they worship the Golden Calf? Rather, their sin occurred so that it would be made clear that one can repent for any sin, as even a sin as severe as the Golden Calf was forgiven.’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Avodah Zarah 4b) to illuminate his exposition here (“And in Avodah Zarah (4b): Israel was not suited for the Golden Calf, as it is said: "O that there were such a heart...", Rashi explaining it was uttered at Sinai, and they lacked only the prayer to plead: "Grant it...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: The delight he then experiences cannot be compared to the delight of one who was never exiled and never tasted poverty at all. Similar teachings appear in the Midrash and the Zohar, as is known. This is the sanctity of Rosh Chodesh: the renewal of the moon's light after it has darkened. It was given to Israel, who are destined to renew themselves like the moon.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 38:2 (§2)
column15: Rather at that hour the Holy One will awaken Abraham and say to him: Arise, for the time has come that I redeem your children to give them good reward for all they suffered in exile; and because Abraham was involved in their original sale/affliction, as written: 'except their Rock had sold them'—this is Abraham, he appears like one in whose eyes it is not yet fitting, etc., saying: collect for their sins, collect for their iniquities, etc., and on this account He says: 'I will say to the north: Give up'.”

column11: Avodah Zarah 5a: ‘The Gemara answers: Do not say that if our ancestors had not sinned we would not have come into the world, as we still would have been born; rather, it would have been as though we had not come into the world. We would have been of no importance, due to the previous generations that would have still been alive. The Gemara asks: Is this to say that if the Jewish people had not sinned with the Golden Calf then they would not have died? But isn’t the chapter that addresses widows whose husbands die childless (Deuteronomy 25:5–10) written in the Torah, and the chapter that addresses the inheritance a deceased father bequeaths to his sons (Numbers 27:8–11) is also written?’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Avodah Zarah 5a) to illuminate his exposition here (“and they lacked only the prayer to plead: "Grant it You!", as the Sages stated (ibid. 5a); and then all they spoke would have been well even in asking to hear from Moses rather than directly from God, although...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column12: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua:17 (§7)
column13: Thus the Book of Joshua is the inscription of wisdom emerging from within the Torah into historical application; which is the territorial order of the Land, operating through natural human effort, while recognizing that all derives solely from the Blessed Name. And this book alongside the Torah would have sufficed had they not sinned, for the entire Oral Torah would have been lucidly apparent to them; requiring only these two external texts: the Torah and the Book of Joshua.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 5:2–3
column15: Therefore they have no genuine spiritual share in the influx. And this is what the holy Ari arranged in the intentions of prayer (Pri Etz Chayyim, Sha'ar Kriyat Shema 1; Sha'ar HaKavanot, Birkat Yotzer): “Who forms servants, and whose servants”—the acronym forms the word 'mum' (blemish). And the explanation is: that they lack the capacity to illuminate those under their charge so that they walk in conscious light.

column11: Eruvin 54a: ‘Rabbi Zeira said that this idea is derived from here: “A man has joy in the answer of his mouth; and a word in due season, how good it is” (Proverbs 15:23). When does a man have joy? When an answer related to Torah study is in his mouth. Another version: When does a man have joy in the answer of his mouth? When he experiences the fulfillment of: A word in due season, how good it is, i.e., when he knows when and how to address each issue.’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Eruvin 54a) to illuminate his exposition here (“although through this they study and forget (Eruvin 54a), requiring the oral toil of Torah, nevertheless through this their heart would have attained greater awe, for awe arises from concealment; wherefore it is...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: And this is “Whereby shall I know” eda—an expression of deep intimate connection, meaning: when he inherits the Land, how will he know and consciously perceive in his wisdom and mind that he is its true heir? That is to say: that he should actively sense the bonding of its sanctity within himself, which is the sanctification of deeds embodied in the sacrificial service.
column15: Meaning that in his power he can gather all creations under his domain, integrating them into himself to stand them upright before the Blessed Name. For in truth holiness resides within all creations, as taught in Eruvin (100b) on Job 35:11: “Rabbi Yochanan said: Had the Torah not been given, we could have learned honesty regarding robbery from the ant, etc.”; yet they lack the power of speech with which to unite with one another, this supreme distinction belonging solely to man, to whom the faculty of speech was given.

column11: Deuteronomy 10:12: ‘And now, O Israel, what does the ETERNAL your God demand of you? Only this: to revere the ETERNAL your God, to walk only in divine paths, to love and to serve the ETERNAL your God with all your heart and soul,’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Deuteronomy 10:12) to illuminate his exposition here (“wherefore it is said: "what does Hashem require of you, but to fear..." [Deuteronomy 10:12], human choice resting on this when God is concealed. And relative to Moses awe is a small thing (Berakhot 33b), he abiding...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: Verse 2: Wisdom (Chochmah) resides in the thought of the brain, while Understanding (Binah) is the will and perception of the heart, as known from the passage Patach Eliyahu. And this is what is placed within human free will, as written: "What does Hashem your God ask of you, but to fear" (Deuteronomy 10:12), which resides in the heart, as stated in Yoma (72b), and in Sanhedrin (106b): "the Merciful One desires the heart," and in I Chronicles (28:9): "for Hashem searches all hearts," and as I wrote elsewhere at length.
column15: Proving that all human acquisition is defined by conscious knowledge. Wherefore this was the purpose of concealment in this world—generating the reality of free choice and labor—so that man might secure eternal reward when Hashem opens His light, still tasting the sweet fulfillment of earned toil. “And shall pitch it within and without with pitch”—this counsel was given corresponding to “and one who forgives his grievances”: meaning that he must pardon his fellow within and without, free of duplicity.

column11: Berakhot 33b: ‘Rabbi Ḥanina waited for him until he completed his prayer. When he finished, Rabbi Ḥanina asked him: Have you concluded all of the praises of your Master? Why do I need all of this superfluous praise? Even these three praises that we recite: The great, mighty and awesome, had Moses our teacher not said them in the Torah and had the members of the Great Assembly not come and incorporated them into the Amida prayer, we would not be permitted to recite them. And you went on and recited all of these. It is comparable to a king who possessed many thousands of golden dinars, yet they were praising him for silver ones. Isn’t that deprecatory? All of the praises we could possibly lavish upon the…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 33b) to illuminate his exposition here (“And relative to Moses awe is a small thing (Berakhot 33b), he abiding in love which Israel attained in the first two Commandments: "Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth" [Song of Songs 1:2]; and through...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: Moses our Teacher, peace be upon him, is the Sun—meaning Heaven—while the fear of Heaven is his bride, which is why our Sages said, "Yes, for Moses it is a small matter", and he acted generously with it, imparting it to Israel. And since this attribute was not internalized within him in the mode of Ani ("I")—for on the contrary, he transcended it as the root of the Torah—his transmission of it to Israel was likewise solely in the mode of union in this world, recognizing Mastership, which represents the arena of human striving.
column15: And since the second Decalogue was spoken after the sin of the Golden Calf through the mouth of Moses our Teacher, according to the capacity of human intellect to receive Torah illumination, and from mortal intellect each commandment appears contradictory to its counterpart, they were delivered with the connecting Vav, hinting that one must maintain constriction and spiritual effort, not extending any commandment to an absolute extreme lest it violate the boundary of its fellow.

column11: Song of Songs 1:2: ‘Oh, give me of the kisses of your mouth, For your love is more delightful than wine.’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Song of Songs 1:2) to illuminate his exposition here (“And relative to Moses awe is a small thing (Berakhot 33b), he abiding in love which Israel attained in the first two Commandments: "Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth" [Song of Songs 1:2]; and through...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: And the Written Torah is merely the unripe fallen fruit of Supernal Wisdom (Bereishit Rabbah 17), and its very essence derives from Gevurah, which is why it is likened unto wine, and it is said: "For your love is better than wine" [Song of Songs 1:2], which they expounded (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1) upon the Oral Torah: that "the words of the Scribes are more beloved etc.," for therein lies the core of divine affection, friendship, and companionship: through the unveiling of sacred mysteries and the placement of the royal seal into his mouth (Shemot Rabbah 41).
column15: And before the Blessed Name, that boundless light transcending all mortal grasp—termed “depths”—already stands wide open. And this very radiance the Blessed Name beamed into the creation of the world even from the Concealed Realm (Alma De-Itkasya); as taught in Tikkunei Zohar (Introduction II, 17b): “‘Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled’ (Song of Songs 5:2)—these represent the first three letters [Yud-Hei-Vav] of the Ineffable Name Havayah, blessed be He.

column11: Malachi 1:6: ‘A son should honor his father, and a slave his master. Now if I were a father, where would be the honor due Me? And if I were a master, where would be the reverence due Me?—said GOD of Hosts to you, O priests who scorn My name. But you ask, “How have we scorned Your name?”’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Malachi 1:6) to illuminate his exposition here (“and through concealment of revelation emerges awe, as a servant to his master: "if I be a master, where is My fear?" [Malachi 1:6], and this is the only treasure the Holy One possesses in His world [Berakhot 33b]....”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: And our Sages expounded "and with great terror" as referring to the revelation of the Shechinah, as written in the gloss of the Rema (Orach Chayim 1:1): when a person takes to heart that Hashem stands over him, awe and submission immediately overtake him. Awe and submission stem from the recognition of His supreme majesty: "if I am a father, where is My honor? And if I am a master, where is My fear?" [Malachi 1:6], honor and awe flowing from acknowledging Him as Father and Sovereign.
column15: And to this our Sages alluded in Eruvin (65a): “Whoever is appeased through his wine possesses of the mind of his Creator.” “Wine” denotes bold certainty; and when Hashem illuminates certainty in the heart that man is a beloved child of God, yet he rests not in that privilege, yielding instead to conduct himself with the humble constriction of a servant before his master—which stirs deeper mercy, fulfilling Malachi 3:17: “as a man spares his own son that serves him” —.

column11: Berakhot 33b: ‘Rabbi Ḥanina waited for him until he completed his prayer. When he finished, Rabbi Ḥanina asked him: Have you concluded all of the praises of your Master? Why do I need all of this superfluous praise? Even these three praises that we recite: The great, mighty and awesome, had Moses our teacher not said them in the Torah and had the members of the Great Assembly not come and incorporated them into the Amida prayer, we would not be permitted to recite them. And you went on and recited all of these. It is comparable to a king who possessed many thousands of golden dinars, yet they were praising him for silver ones. Isn’t that deprecatory? All of the praises we could possibly lavish upon the…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 33b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and this is the only treasure the Holy One possesses in His world [Berakhot 33b]. But: "O that there were such a heart in them to fear...", that they never sever that awe, and had they answered "Grant it You!", they...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: And from this too [we learn] that the portion was written for their praise — for if it were for his disgrace, God forbid, in its plain sense, what proof is there from the yud that “cried out”? For [the yud] merited to be in the name of that righteous woman [Sarah], and it is right that it stand and cry over being lowered from its elevation, taken from there; not so that [Bathsheba] portion, which speaks, God forbid, in disgrace of that tzaddik — [where] on the contrary it would be praise and satisfaction for those letters not to be written! But in truth it is fitting for him from the six days of Creation, as it is [explained] there.
column15: “These are the generations of the heaven and of the earth when they were created, in the day that the Lord God made the earth and the heavens.” “Heaven” denotes that which the Blessed Name bestows in His sheer goodness without human toil, which is the portion of Moses our Teacher, termed “Shabbat.” Therefore Moses instituted the blessing “Who feeds the entire world in His goodness” (Berakhot 48b), and in Moses' merit the manna fell from heaven.

column11: Berakhot 28b: ‘His students said to him: Our teacher, bless us. He said to them: May it be His will that the fear of Heaven shall be upon you like the fear of flesh and blood. His students were puzzled and said: To that point and not beyond? Shouldn’t one fear God more? He said to them: Would that a person achieve that level of fear. Know that when one commits a transgression, he says to himself: I hope that no man will see me. If one is as concerned about avoiding shame before God as he is before man, he will never sin.’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 28b) to illuminate his exposition here (“as in Berakhot (28b): "May the fear of Heaven be upon you like the fear of flesh and blood, for when a man sins he says: Let no man see me"; and they would have merited the perfection of the Oral Torah: "if the fear...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: Which stems from shame before the sight of flesh and blood; and one who possesses true fear of Heaven feels bashful before Hashem to transgress. And noble shame does not arise from degraded self-effacement, for the basest individuals possess no shame, rather authentic shame exists in proportion to dignity and stature.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:11
column15: And as explained in Parashat Bereishit s.v. "Na'aseh Adam" (above, Parashat Bereishit, letters 39, 40). For the constitution of man himself is assembled from multiple opposing and distinct forces: flesh and blood, bones and sinews, fire, air, water, and earth; and were it not for the utterance of Hashem's mouth uniting them and sustaining them, behold, each elemental foundation would then scatter to its element, and the structure of man would be dismantled.

column11: Shabbat 31b: ‘fear of Heaven is like a treasurer [gizbar] to whom they gave keys to the inner doors of the treasury but they did not give keys to the outer door. With what key will he enter? Although the Torah is the inner key, without fear of Heaven one cannot gain access to the genuine Torah. Similarly, Rabbi Yannai would proclaim: Woe unto one who does not have a courtyard, and who makes a fence for the courtyard, i.e., a person who lacks fear of Heaven and is nevertheless involved in Torah study. Rav Yehuda said: The Holy One, Blessed be He, only created His world so that people would fear before Him, as it is stated: “And God has so made it that men should fear before Him” (Ecclesiastes 3:14).’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 31b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and they would have merited the perfection of the Oral Torah: "if the fear of Hashem is his treasure, yes; if not, no" [Shabbat 31b]. And suspending the mountain like a vat occurred because it was revealed before Him...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: Therefore one's fear of sin must precede his wisdom, as stated in Avot, for otherwise it cannot endure, and "if there is no fear, there is no wisdom." And this explains why the Talmud in Shabbat first likened it to outer keys, and then conversely likened fear to the inner courtyard and Torah to the outer gate, which appears contradictory—presenting fear as inner and Torah as the entryway—alongside the mishnaic dictum in Avot: "If there is no wisdom, there is no fear."
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 15:3
column15: And from this is born in man a desire for fulfilling the mitzvot, the overarching principle of which is “You shall love your neighbor as yourself”, as brought in Shabbat (31a): “What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow; this is the entire Torah”; and it branches from the realization that one God created us, one Maker formed us all; wherefore one must love his fellow and anticipate his welfare.

column11: Avodah Zarah 5b: ‘Yet even Moses our teacher, who said this to the Jewish people, did not allude to the Jewish people until after forty years that they should have stated this request, as it is stated: “And I have led you forty years in the wilderness” (Deuteronomy 29:4), which shows that Moses was speaking forty years after the revelation at Sinai. And at that point it is written: “But the Lord has not given you a heart to know, and eyes to see, and ears to hear, until this day” (Deuteronomy 29:3). Rabba said: Conclude from here that a person does not understand the opinion of his teacher until after forty years, as Moses said this to the Jewish people only after forty years of learning Torah.’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Avodah Zarah 5b) to illuminate his exposition here (“And even Moses did not fathom his Master's mind to instruct them until forty years ended (Avodah Zarah 5b); for he too assumed Hashem willed subduing the inclination through mortal exertion, hence the mountain's...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: And since after forty years they merited a heart to know, and as they derived (Avodah Zarah 5b) from this verse: infer from this: a person does not fully grasp the mind of his master until forty years have elapsed, consequently they merited then that there were given to them eyes to see and ears to hear as explained.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 55:8–9
column15: And these utterances are an ongoing prophecy for every generation and every individual Jewish soul, to know how Hashem engages with every single soul of Israel. And although the entire Torah constitutes prophetic pathways to understand the engagement Hashem maintains with His people Israel, nonetheless here is Hashem's prophecy revealed most explicitly within the mystery of the Tetragrammaton (Havayah): The first utterance points to the letter Yud of the Name Havayah.

column11: Psalms 51:17: ‘O my Sovereign, open my lips,and let my mouth declare Your praise.’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Psalms 51:17) to illuminate his exposition here (“prayer itself proceeding from Hashem, wherefore we recite "Hashem, open my lips" before praying, "fluent prayer" (Berakhot 34b) meaning dispatched from Above; and had they been worthy, they would have been inspired...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: Requiring no repetition thereafter, like "Hashem, open my lips, and my mouth shall declare Your praise"—divine opening being needed at the difficult beginning, after which speech flows on its own, mirroring "Turn us unto You, Hashem, and we shall be turned," great assistance being required for the inception. Therefore an obligatory eating was instituted then that exists nowhere else in the year, eating imparting actual, revealed vitality; and when it is a mitzvah meal, holy vitality is infused within him, which vitalizes speech, the power of manifest actuality.
column15: “In the beginning God created.” It is stated in Midrash Rabbah (Bereishit 9:2): The Holy One, blessed be He, was building worlds and destroying them, saying: “These do not please Me; this one pleases Me.” And this is alluded to in the word “Elohim,” for the Name Elohim corresponds to all arduous spiritual services, as it is said (Psalms 51:19): “A broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise,” “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit.”

column11: Berakhot 34b: ‘MISHNA: Concluding its discussion of the halakhot of prayer, the mishna discusses less practical aspects of prayer. One who prays and realizes that he erred in his prayer, it is a bad omen for him; it indicates to him that his prayer was not accepted. And if he who erred is the communal prayer leader, it is a bad omen for those who sent him, because a person’s agent has legal status equivalent to his own. On a similar note, they said about Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa that he would pray on behalf of the sick and immediately after his prayer he would say: This one shall recover from his illness and live and this one shall die. When they said to him: From where do you know? He said to them: If my…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 34b) to illuminate his exposition here (“"fluent prayer" (Berakhot 34b) meaning dispatched from Above; and had they been worthy, they would have been inspired from Heaven to pray for this; and of this it is said: "Yet Hashem has not given you a heart to...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: Such is His divine way: when He desires to bring salvation, He places within that person's heart to cry out unto Him. And this is the reason for the teaching (Berakhot 34b): "If my prayer is fluent in my mouth, I know it is accepted," for when it is destined to effect salvation, the prayer is sent and fluently dispatched into his mouth from the Blessed Name.
column15: The explanation of this is: the Blessed Name is abundant in lovingkindness, and if a person sins in matters strictly between man and God, the sin would be pardoned immediately, affecting no creature and leaving none to stand and prosecute against him. As in Tanna Devei Eliyahu (Rabbah 6): Even if a man committed one hundred sins, one greater than the other, and repented, the Holy One says: “Behold, I am with him in mercy” — meaning if a person prays a single prayer from the depth of his heart, all sins between man and God are pardoned immediately.

column11: Deuteronomy 29:3: ‘Yet to this day GOD has not given you a mind to understand or eyes to see or ears to hear.’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Deuteronomy 29:3) to illuminate his exposition here (“and of this it is said: "Yet Hashem has not given you a heart to know..." [Deuteronomy 29:3], Hashem not having yet granted them this discerning heart, which caused Moses likewise not to stir them to request it. And...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: And the connection of this to circumcision is based on that which is stated: “Yet Hashem has not given you a heart to know, and eyes to see, and ears to hear, etc., and I have led you, etc., bread you have not eaten, neither have you drunk wine or strong drink, etc.,” (Deuteronomy 29:3–5), meaning that once He granted them a heart to know, they then merited having eyes to see, namely that they see only Hashem and learn from all creations for His holy service.
column15: Israel, however, existed, they exist now, and they are destined to exist eternally: They existed—as it is written (Psalms 74:2): ‘Remember Your congregation, which You acquired of old (kedem)’—before the world was created; and they exist now—as it is said (Deuteronomy 29:9): ‘You stand this day all of you’; and they are destined to exist in the World to Come—as it is said (Malachi 3:17): ‘And they shall be Mine, says the Lord of hosts, in that day when I make up My jewels.’

column11: Esther 3:14: ‘The text of the document was to the effect that a law should be proclaimed in every single province; it was to be publicly displayed to all the peoples, so that they might be ready for that day.’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Esther 3:14) to illuminate his exposition here (“as with Haman's decree: "to be ready against that day" [Esther 3:14], which was inverted into the Jews being ready against that day to avenge themselves [ibid. 8:13], bringing immense destruction upon Amalek and...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: And this occurs when one yields to the accuser, whereas one who comes to be elevated must offer his soul-ransom unto Hashem, that the prosecutor may have no dominion over him. And this is the coin of fire: instilling holiness into all materiality until the title "Holy" is designated even upon the shekel and the inanimate coin; operating through awakening the root of truth in the initial thought, wherein the culmination of action is embedded; and against that inner point of truth no prosecution can ever stand.
column15: As taught in Chullin (139b): Where is Haman alluded to in the Torah? In: “Hamin ha-etz...” — the question being: from where did such dark concealment arise that Israel feared Haman's decree of annihilation? And the Gemara resolves: “Hamin ha-etz”—this concealment stems from the sin of Adam, where Hashem cast doubt in his heart lest he transgressed His words.

column11: Esther 8:13: “‘The copy of the writing, to be given out for a decree in every province, was published unto all the peoples, that the Jews should be ready against that day (atihdim la-yom ha-zeh) to avenge themselves on their enemies.’” Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Esther 8:13) to illuminate his exposition here (“which was inverted into the Jews being ready against that day to avenge themselves [ibid. 8:13], bringing immense destruction upon Amalek and establishing the feast for all generations "until one knows not" [Megillah...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: There are four commandments on Purim: reading the Megillah, sending portions one to another, gifts to the needy, and the festive meal of drinking and joy (Esther 9:22); and certainly they were ordained to channel through them upon the person the holiness of the day; just as there was then unto the Jews four blessings: "light, and gladness, and joy, and honor" (Esther 8:16); and to effect through them the blotting out of Amalek in every particular detail, countering a specific aspect and level of Amalek's powers.
column15: And surely Hashem never repents of His deeds, for He is not a man that He should repent; rather, His Will was to create them so that their collapse would instill awe in succeeding generations, restraining them from reckless expansion. For such is the divine architecture of creation: the first world possessed bold certainty, collapsing when expanding excessively, through whose failure the next world gained the awe to exercise restraint, progressing toward the World of Rectification—this being the “second child.”

column11: Megillah 7b: ‘Rava said: A Purim feast that one ate at night did not fulfill his obligation. What is the reason? “Days of feasting and gladness” (Esther 9:22) is written, i.e., days and not nights. The Gemara relates: Rav Ashi was sitting before Rav Kahana his teacher on Purim, and it grew dark and the Sages who usually came to study with him did not come. column11: Yoma 72b: ‘Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: What is the meaning of that which is written: “And this is the Torah which Moses put [sam] before the children of Israel” (Deuteronomy 4:44)? The word sam is written with the letter sin and means put; it is phonetically similar to the word sam written with the letter samekh, meaning a drug. This use of this word therefore alludes to the following: If one is deserving, the Torah becomes a potion [sam] of life for him. If one is not deserving, the Torah becomes a potion of death for him. And this idea is what Rava said: For one who is skillful in his study of Torah and immerses himself in it with love, it is a potion of life; but for one who is not skillful in…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Yoma 72b) to illuminate his exposition here (“if he merits, it becomes an elixir of life [ibid. 72b], reaching the Tree of Life. column11: Sanhedrin 24a: ‘The Gemara cites another example of Torah scholars who spoke of each other with reverence. It is like that incident where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sat and said: It is prohibited to insulate cold food on Shabbat to keep it cold, as this may lead one to insulate hot food on Shabbat to keep it hot. Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, said before him: My father ruled that it is permitted to insulate cold food on Shabbat. There is no concern that this will lead one to insulate hot food on Shabbat. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi subsequently said to those who asked him about this issue: I retract my previous statement; the elder, Rabbi Yosei, has already issued a ruling on this topic, and I defer to his ruling.’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 24a) to illuminate his exposition here (“the ruling that Sinai is superior reflecting the learning of the Land of Israel who are pleasant to each other in halakhah (Sanhedrin 24a), and Rabbi Zeira fasted one hundred fasts to forget the Babylonian dialectic...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.

column11: Bava Metzia 85a: ‘The Gemara relates a similar occurrence: When Rabbi Zeira ascended from Babylonia to Eretz Yisrael, he fasted one hundred fasts so that he would forget the Babylonian method of studying Gemara, so that it would not hinder him from adapting to the unique style of study prevalent in Eretz Yisrael. He fasted an additional one hundred fasts so that Rabbi Elazar, ben Pedat, would not die during his lifetime, which would have caused the burden of communal matters to fall upon him. As dean of the Torah academy, Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat was in charge of all public affairs, leaving Rabbi Zeira unencumbered to study Torah. Rabbi Zeira fasted an additional one hundred fasts so that the fire of…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Metzia 85a) to illuminate his exposition here (“and Rabbi Zeira fasted one hundred fasts to forget the Babylonian dialectic (Bava Metzia 85a), assigning superiority to Mishnah; whereas Rava, founding pillar of the Babylonian dialectic (the debates of Abaye and...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.

column11: Sukkah 28a: ‘Apropos the character traits of Rabbi Eliezer, the Gemara cites character traits of his teacher. column11: Sanhedrin 86a: ‘The Gemara responds: That should not enter your mind, as the unattributed baraita that was cited is a passage from the halakhic midrash on the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy entitled Sifrei, and Rabbi Yoḥanan says: An unattributed mishna is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Meir; an unattributed baraita in the Tosefta is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Neḥemya; an unattributed baraita in the Sifra, the halakhic midrash on the book of Leviticus, is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda; and an unattributed baraita in the Sifrei is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Shimon. And all of these are in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Akiva, as all the Sages…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 86a) to illuminate his exposition here (“An anonymous Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir (Sanhedrin 86a), in whose scroll was written garments of light (or) with an Aleph (Bereishit Rabbah 20:12), illuminating the halakhah (Eruvin 13b), his colleagues being unable...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: While in the Torah scroll of Rabbi Meir it was written "garments of light" (kasnos or with an aleph), as they stated [in Bereishis Rabbah 20:12]. And therefore he was able to demonstrate reasons to declare the impure pure and the pure impure (Eruvin 13b); for this derives from perceiving the hidden root of every single thing: for every created thing is an admixture of good and evil, and the governance of this world is according to its manifestation in this world, which is finite and bounded.
column15: And for this reason, in the generation of King Hezekiah and the generation of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai a rainbow was never seen in their lifetimes (Bereishit Rabbah 35:2); because they embodied the connective Vav, illuminating through their deeds so that such dense darkness never enveloped the world, rendering the sign of the rainbow unnecessary.

column11: Bereshit Rabbah 20:12: ‘“The Lord God made for Adam and for his wife garments of hide [or],. and clothed them” (Genesis 3:21). In Rabbi Meir’s Torah, they found that “garments of or”, meaning light. was written. These are the garments of Adam the first man, that were similar to the common rue, broad at the bottom and narrow at the top. Rabbi Yitzḥak Ravya says: They were as smooth as a fingernail and as pretty as jewels. Rabbi Yitzḥak said: It was like the thin linen garments that come from Beit She’an. [And they were called] garments of hide because they adhered to the skin. Rabbi Elazar said: Goat hides. Rabbi Aivu said: Garments that cover the skin. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: Hare hides. Rabbi Yosei bar…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 20:12) to illuminate his exposition here (“An anonymous Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir (Sanhedrin 86a), in whose scroll was written garments of light (or) with an Aleph (Bereishit Rabbah 20:12), illuminating the halakhah (Eruvin 13b), his colleagues being unable...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: And this is the mystery of: 'garments of light (or)' spelled with an Aleph which was written in the Torah scroll of Rabbi Meir (Bereishit Rabbah 20:12), as will be in the future: spiritual light in place of the body's skin (or with an Ayin); and if so, shattering does not apply at all, nor mortality. And along the lines of what Rabbeinu Sa'adyah Gaon wrote in the Book of Beliefs and Opinions (Treatise 7) regarding those consumed by lions or burnt in fire, etc..
column15: As taught in the Zohar (Kedoshim 83b) in Sitrei Torah: Primordial Adam held nothing of this physical world; the Righteous One united with His Female and formed a body whose radiance surpassed the ministering angels on high, etc.; once he sinned he was drawn down, diminished, and needed another body of skin and flesh, as written: “And the Lord God made for Adam and his wife coats of skin, and clothed them”—which is Adam of Asiyah (Action).

column11: Eruvin 13b: ‘On the topic of Rabbi Meir and his Torah study, the Gemara cites an additional statement. Rabbi Aḥa bar Ḥanina said: It is revealed and known before the One Who spoke and the world came into being that in the generation of Rabbi Meir there was no one of the Sages who is his equal. Why then didn’t the Sages establish the halakha in accordance with his opinion? It is because his colleagues were unable to ascertain the profundity of his opinion. He was so brilliant that he could present a cogent argument for any position, even if it was not consistent with the prevalent halakha. As he would state with regard to a ritually impure item that it is pure, and display justification for that…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Eruvin 13b) to illuminate his exposition here (“An anonymous Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir (Sanhedrin 86a), in whose scroll was written garments of light (or) with an Aleph (Bereishit Rabbah 20:12), illuminating the halakhah (Eruvin 13b), his colleagues being unable...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: And beholding King David, peace be upon him, and comprehending him—or in his lifetime gazing upon his physical visage, akin to the dictum "I am sharp because I saw Rabbi Meir" (Eruvin 13b): "they looked at his mouth"— as written: "And thine eyes shall see thy teachers", and as I wrote elsewhere concerning this, that the essence of the soul resides within the face, matching "their facial features do not resemble one another" (Sanhedrin 38a) due to the diversification of souls, whereas such distinction is not visible across the entire body, which serves merely as a garment for the soul.
column15: “All in whose nostrils was the breath of life, of all that was in the dry land, died.” It is taught in Tractate Sanhedrin (108a): “And not the fish of the sea.” The root of this matter is: although fish are more naturally prone to promiscuity than all creatures (Bava Batra 74b: “fish are uninhibited”), such that strict justice would dictate that fish perish before all other creatures; yet they were spared because they possess no moral free will, dwelling within the water which symbolizes the Concealed Realm (Alma De-Itkasya), their root above being in the Holy Ancient One (Atika Kadisha).

column11: Bava Metzia 84b: ‘As a result of that incident, the relationship of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi changed. Up until that day, when Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi would state a matter of Torah, Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, would support him by citing proofs for his opinion. From this point forward, when they were discussing a subject and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi would say: I have an argument to respond, Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, would preempt him by saying to him: Such and such is what you have to respond, and this is the refutation of your claim. Now that you asked these questions, you have surrounded us with bundles of refutations that have no substance, i.e., you have forced…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Metzia 84b) to illuminate his exposition here (“his colleagues being unable to fathom his full depth (ibid.), his light remaining concealed; but Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai merited to unveil the hidden light in the Zohar. Wherefore in Gittin (67a) he stated his...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: And [Korach and his assembly] came to dispute his authority with the argument: "all the congregation are holy... wherefore then lift ye up yourselves?" (Bamidbar 16:3); meaning that a Torah scholar has no superiority over an am ha'aretz, for "Your people are all righteous" and inherit the earth and the World to Come; for even the empty ones of Israel are as full of mitzvos as a pomegranate as they said [in Berachos 57a], which refers to an am ha'aretz who is empty of Torah knowledge.

column15: And this corresponds to what is taught in the Talmud (Megillah 19b): “Had there remained from the cave in which Moses and Elijah stood as much as the eye of a fine needle (machat sidkit), they would not have been able to endure before the radiant light.” And to understand: why did the Gemara specify the eye of a fine stitching needle, and why not use a more extreme metaphor: 'the point of a needle', saying that even such a minuscule measure did not remain?!

column11: Gittin 67a: ‘This is as it is taught in a baraita that Isi ben Yehuda would recount the praise of the Sages by characterizing each of them: Rabbi Meir, a scholar and scribe; Rabbi Yehuda, a scholar when he chooses to be one; Rabbi Tarfon, a pile of nuts, as, just as when one removes a nut from a pile all the other nuts fall, so too, when a student would ask Rabbi Tarfon with regard to one matter, he would cite sources from all the disciplines of the Torah; Rabbi Yishmael, a well-stocked store; Rabbi Akiva, a full storehouse; Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri, a peddler’s basket, in which there is a small amount of each product; Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, a basket of fragrant spices, as everything he says is…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Gittin 67a) to illuminate his exposition here (“Wherefore in Gittin (67a) he stated his measures were distilled tithes from the measures of Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Akiva being the root of the entire Oral Torah including exoteric law, and Rashbi taught the distilled...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: And this is what is stated in Gittin 67a: Rabbi Meir is a sage and a scribe; “scribe” alludes to the perfection of the physical material, which was likewise at the absolute summit of refinement, meaning that even all material details entered into holiness under wisdom; and this is: Rabbi Meir takes the minority into account, to rectify even the minutest fragment within physical matter; and therefore he examined names which correspond to material substance.
column15: It is taught in the Gemara (Rosh Hashanah 31a): It was taught in a baraita: Rabbi Yehudah says in the name of Rabbi Akiva: On the first day of the week, what did the Levites recite? “The earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof” (Psalms 24:1)—because He acquired, imparted possession, and ruled over His world.

column11: Bava Batra 12a: ‘§ In connection with Rabbi Yosei’s statement that Sumakhos’s words are nothing but words of prophecy, the Gemara reports that Rabbi Avdimi from Haifa says: From the day that the Temple was destroyed prophecy was taken from the prophets and given to the Sages. The Gemara expresses astonishment: Is that to say that a Sage is not fit to be a prophet? Rabbi Avdimi seems to say that these are two distinct categories of people. The Gemara explains: This is what Rabbi Avdimi is saying: Even though prophecy was taken from the prophets, it was not taken from the Sages.’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Batra 12a) to illuminate his exposition here (“as in Bava Batra (12a) that prophecy was not taken from sages, hitting upon Sinai halakhah through intellect, being superior to a prophet whose grasp is limited to his attribute, Hod sheb'Hod being the prophetic...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: Which is achieved solely through his adherence to the hevela de-garmei, whereby he binds also to the echoing voice and prophecy. And although none attained this consciously except David and Solomon, nonetheless every scholar merits this at times through Chochmah [which is why prophecy was given "to the sages"], which is entirely concealed in its root as written above, and this explains why the sage arrives at the ruling "without giving a rational reason," having reached it through intuitive supernal Wisdom.
column15: And separation indicates that the transcendent realm is completely set apart from mortal reach; for man cannot legitimately penetrate what lies beyond the boundary of his intellect; only within the perimeter of his conscious grasp has God permitted him to walk, serving his Creator through discernment, discipline, and refined character traits; whereas if he attempts to trespass into what lies beyond his designated pale, he will be utterly destroyed.

column13: And Matisyahu, who overcame them, it is known in Sefer Pri Etz Chaim that he repaired the Hod — therefore we say “for the miracles” in the blessing of thanksgiving [Hoda’ah]; and he was a priest, and his seed merited the kingship, even though they were punished for it — because they were priests and took the monarchy, as the Ramban wrote [Parashas Vayechi] on the verse “the scepter shall not depart [from Yehudah].”: normally Malchus (Rachel) receives the light of Hod only via Netzach (since “Hod was turned to ruin,” Daniel 10:8, while “Netzach Yisrael does not lie,” Shmuel I 15:29); but “Matisyahu ben Yochanan the High Priest repaired the Hod” in these…
column15: For the sun and moon truly hold power to govern the physical world (“strength and might He placed within them to rule in the midst of the world”); because they possess permanent, humble awareness that all strength is in Hashem's hand alone, as in Zohar Pinchas (257b): every divine Name whose bearer acknowledges that no creature holds power, receives governance: Adonai testifies He is Master of all worlds, Din (judgment) permuting to Adonai; The Name El bears witness to the Master of all that no Name, existence or level has power, all the more so any lesser creature, as it is written (Daniel 4:32): “And all the inhabitants of the earth are accounted as nothing.”

column11: Numbers 24:20: ‘He saw Amalek and, taking up his theme, he said:A leading nation is Amalek;But its fate is to perish forever.’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 6, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Numbers 24:20) to illuminate his exposition here (“through the surge of the unholy counterpart—Haman under Persia, of Amalek the "first of the nations," the root of all gentile wisdom; regarding which it is said: "shall I not destroy the wise men out of Edom, and...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.
column13: As Haman’s “accusation” was over what they [Israel] had done “only outwardly [lifnim]” in bowing to the image [in Nevuchadnetzar’s day], as the Sages said (Megillah 12a)], and so [Hashem] too dealt with them only outwardly [and did not truly destroy them]. — for he [Amalek] is “the first of the nations” (Bamidbar 24:20), and the “beginning of the spreading-forth” is Midyan — and this is the “beginning of evil.”
column15: For the supreme revelation of Hashem's greatness in this world is that He cloaked His light in garments of darkness, yet the light breaks through every veil; therefore one who partakes of physical bounty as the nations do, taking without restraint and without a blessing— which alludes to the years of youthful expansiveness in a person before attaining maturity— and afterward the Blessed Name grants him the conscious wisdom to praise Him for it; for upon sight alone one does not recite a blessing over sustenance, but only upon tasting, even though while tasting one is momentarily distracted.
